pages.subject: The event update
paragraphs: The update is being prepared on Thursday 3 December 2026. The event has moved from Friday 4 December to Monday 7 December. The start time remains 10 am, and the room remains room 2.
Recipients must confirm whether they can attend by 5 pm on Friday 4 December. They are being asked to confirm attendance, not merely acknowledge that they have read the update.

pages.subject: The same facts for two audiences
paragraphs: The client version opens formally: “I’m writing to let you know that the event has been rescheduled.” The friend version begins: “Quick update: the event has moved.”
Both versions give Monday 7 December, 10 am, room 2 and the Friday 4 December 5 pm attendance deadline. The tone changes with the relationship; the event details and requested action do not.

pages.title: Listen and answer
pages.instruction: Acknowledgement is not attendance. Listen for the new information and decide how to respond
pages.message: Hi, Ana. I’ve read the event update, but I’m not sure what you need from me. When you say “please acknowledge”, do you only want me to confirm I’ve seen the message, or do you need to know whether I can attend on Monday? I can send either, but they aren’t the same commitment. Could you also give the response deadline as a day and time rather than “tomorrow”? I sometimes read messages after the day they were sent. The new date, same ten o’clock start and room two are clear. It’s the requested action that needs clarification, so there’s no need to rewrite every factual detail or make the wording more elaborate
pages.audioText: Hi, Ana. I’ve read the event update, but I’m not sure what you need from me. s_mission.title: Same update, different tone

questions.prompt: Which opening is used in the message to the client?
questions.answer: The client message opens, “I’m writing to let you know that the event has been rescheduled.”
questions.hint: Find the opening explicitly identified as the client version.

questions.prompt: What changed, and which two event details stayed the same?
questions.answer: The date changed to Monday 7 December; the 10 am start and room 2 stayed the same.
questions.hint: Distinguish the new date from the unchanged time and room.

questions.prompt: What must recipients confirm, and by when?
questions.answer: They must confirm attendance by 5 pm on Friday 4 December.
questions.hint: Find the requested action and deadline, not just the event date.

referenceParagraphs: The client message opens, “I’m writing to let you know that the event has been rescheduled.” The friend message begins, “Quick update: the event has moved.”
Both say that the event has moved from Friday 4 December to Monday 7 December 2026. It still starts at 10 am in room 2. Both ask recipients to confirm attendance by 5 pm on Friday 4 December.

s_reply.title: Receipt or attendance?

questions.prompt: Which event details has the recipient already understood?
questions.answer: They have understood Monday 7 December, 10 am and room 2.
questions.hint: Find the information that does not need explaining again.

questions.prompt: What distinction is the recipient unsure about?
questions.answer: They are unsure whether to acknowledge reading the message or confirm attendance.
questions.hint: Look for the two possible interpretations.

questions.prompt: Why would “I’ve read this” be insufficient?
questions.answer: It would not confirm whether the recipient will attend.
questions.hint: Compare a read receipt with the sender’s actual request.

referenceParagraphs: The recipient has understood the new date, Monday 7 December, and the unchanged time and place: 10 am in room 2. However, they are unsure whether the sender wants a read receipt or confirmation that they will attend.
The sender needs confirmation of attendance by 5 pm on Friday 4 December. A message saying only “I’ve read this” would not answer that request.
